---
title: "1. Continuous integration: automatically running unit tests"
order: 1
---

In this tutorial you will add unit tests to a simple Python package, then
write a GitHub Actions workflow that automatically runs those tests every time
you open or update a pull request. This is known as *continuous integration*
(CI). Nearly every open source project of any size uses some form of CI, since
it lets maintainers know right away whether a contribution breaks anything.

For this exercise we'll use a toy Python package that I created called
[`toymath`](https://github.com/SU-OSPO/toymath). It contains a couple of
functions for doing (very) simple math.

## I. Set up the repository

### 1. Fork, clone, and create a branch

:::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" icon="false"}
#### Challenge

Use what you learned in the [git and GitHub tutorials](../02_git/index.qmd) to:

1.  Create a fork of https://github.com/SU-OSPO/toymath under your GitHub account.

2.  Clone **your fork** to your local computer.

3.  In your local repository, create and switch to a new branch called `add-ci-tests`.

Try to do this on your own. If you can't remember how, refer back to
[Part 2](../02_git/cli/exercise2.qmd) and [Part 3](../02_git/cli/exercise3.qmd)
of the git tutorials. If you're still stuck, expand the solution below.

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false"}
##### Solution

1.  Go to https://github.com/SU-OSPO/toymath and click the `Fork` button in the
    upper right. On the "Create a new fork" page, select **your username** under
    "Owner" and leave the repository name as `toymath`. Click the green
    `Create fork` button. You'll be redirected to your fork, which will have a
    URL like `https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/toymath`.

2.  On your fork's webpage, click the green `<> Code` button, select the "SSH"
    tab, and copy the URL. It should look like
    `git@github.com:YOUR_USERNAME/toymath.git`. Then, in a terminal, `cd` to the
    directory you'd like to keep the repository in and run:

    ```bash
    git clone git@github.com:YOUR_USERNAME/toymath.git
    cd toymath
    ```

    (If you're using VS Code for authentication instead of an SSH key, copy the
    HTTPS URL instead and use the "Git: Clone" command in the command palette,
    as described in [Part 2](../02_git/cli/exercise2.qmd#if-you-are-using-vs-code)
    of the git tutorials.)

3.  Run:

    ```bash
    git checkout -b add-ci-tests
    ```

    You can verify you're on the new branch by running `git branch`.
:::
::::

Take a look around the repository. The package's source code is in the
`toymath` directory. The functions we care about are in
`toymath/functions.py`:

```python
"""Basic arithmetic functions."""


def add(a, b):
    """Return the sum of a and b."""
    return a + b


def subtract(a, b):
    """Return a minus b."""
    return a - b
```

There's also a `pyproject.toml` file, which tells `pip` how to install the
package (we covered this in the [packaging and deployment
lecture](../04_packaging_deployment/index.qmd)). Notice what's *not* there:
any tests!

### 2. Create a conda environment and install `toymath`

Let's create a new conda environment to develop `toymath` in. From the
`toymath` directory, run:

```bash
conda create -n toymath python=3.13
conda activate toymath
```

Now install `toymath` into the environment:

```bash
pip install -e .
```

The `.` tells `pip` to install the package in the current directory. The `-e`
flag installs it in *editable* mode. This means that rather than copying the
source code into your environment, `pip` points the environment to the source
code in your repository. That way, any changes you make to the code will be
picked up immediately, without having to re-install the package. This is what
you usually want to do when developing a package.

To check that the install worked, try out the command-line program that comes
with `toymath`:

```bash
toymath_calculator add 2 3
```

You should get back `5.0`.

## II. Write and run unit tests

### 3. Write a test

We'll use [`pytest`](https://docs.pytest.org) to test our code. `pytest` looks
for files whose names start with `test_`, then runs any function in those files
whose name starts with `test_`. If the function runs without error, the test
passes. If it raises an error, the test fails. Typically, tests use Python's
`assert` statement to check that a function returns what we expect; `assert`
will raise an error if the statement following it is `False`.

1.  In the top level of your repository, create a directory called `tests`:

    ```bash
    mkdir tests
    ```

2.  Use your favorite text editor to create a file called `tests/test_functions.py`
    and put the following in it:

    ```python
    """Unit tests for the functions in toymath."""

    from toymath import add, subtract


    def test_add_subtract_roundtrip():
        """Check that subtracting a from the sum of a and b gives back b."""
        for a, b in [(3, 5), (-2, 7), (10, 0)]:
            c = add(a, b)
            assert subtract(c, a) == b
    ```

    This is called a *round-trip* test: we add two numbers `a` and `b` to get
    `c`, then subtract `a` from `c`. If both `add` and `subtract` are working
    correctly, we should get back `b`. We do this for a few different pairs of
    numbers to make sure it isn't working just by chance.

### 4. Run the tests

1.  Install `pytest` into your environment:

    ```bash
    pip install pytest
    ```

    ::: {.callout-tip}
    Take a look at `pyproject.toml`. You'll see a `[project.optional-dependencies]`
    section with `test = ["pytest"]`. This is a common way to list the extra
    packages that developers need to run the tests. Instead of installing
    `pytest` directly, you could have run `pip install -e ".[test]"`, which would
    install `toymath` along with everything in the `test` list.
    :::

2.  From the top level of your repository, run:

    ```bash
    pytest
    ```

    `pytest` will find your test and run it. You should see something like:

    ```bash
    ============================= test session starts ==============================
    ...
    collected 1 item

    tests/test_functions.py .                                                [100%]

    ============================== 1 passed in 0.01s ===============================
    ```

    The `.` after the file name means the test passed. Congratulations, you've
    written and run your first unit test!

3.  Commit your new test:

    ```bash
    git add tests/test_functions.py
    git commit -m "add round-trip test for add and subtract"
    ```

## III. Create a GitHub workflow to run the tests

Running the tests on your own computer is great, but it relies on everyone
remembering to do it. It also only tells you whether the tests pass on *your*
computer, with *your* operating system and *your* version of Python. Let's have
GitHub run the tests for us automatically.

GitHub Actions are configured by *workflow* files. These are
[YAML](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YAML) files that live in the
`.github/workflows` directory of your repository. GitHub automatically looks
for files in that directory and runs them when the conditions you specify are
met.

We'll write the workflow by hand so that you can see what each part does.
For more details than are given here, see GitHub's
[Creating an example workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/create-an-example-workflow)
tutorial.

### 5. Write the workflow file

1.  Create the `.github/workflows` directory. From the top level of your repository run:

    ```bash
    mkdir -p .github/workflows
    ```

    (Note the `.` at the start of `.github`! Since it starts with a `.`, it is
    a hidden directory; you'll need to run `ls -a` to see it.)

2.  Use your favorite text editor to create a file called
    `.github/workflows/tests.yml`. We'll build it up a piece at a time.

3.  First, give the workflow a name and tell GitHub when to run it. Add the
    following to `tests.yml`:

    ```yaml
    name: Tests

    on:
      push:
        branches: [main]
      pull_request:
    ```

    The `name` is what will show up on GitHub when the workflow runs. The `on`
    section lists the *events* that trigger the workflow. Here we've said to
    run the workflow whenever anything is pushed to the `main` branch, and
    whenever a pull request is opened or updated. (There are many other
    events you can trigger on; see
    [Events that trigger workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows)
    for the full list.)

    ::: {.callout-warning}
    Indentation matters in YAML! It's how YAML knows what belongs to what.
    Always use spaces, never tabs, and be consistent. If your workflow doesn't
    run, the first thing to check is your indentation.
    :::

4.  Next, add a *job*. A workflow is made up of one or more jobs, each of
    which runs on its own fresh computer (a *runner*). Add the following below
    what you have:

    ```yaml

    jobs:
      test:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    ```

    `test` is the ID of the job; you can call it whatever you like.
    `runs-on` tells GitHub what operating system to use for the runner. Here
    we're using the latest version of Ubuntu Linux that GitHub provides.

5.  Finally, tell the job what to do by giving it a list of *steps*. Add the
    following under `runs-on` (note the indentation: `steps` should line up
    with `runs-on`):

    ```yaml
        steps:
          - name: Check out the repository
            uses: actions/checkout@v7

          - name: Set up Python
            uses: actions/setup-python@v7
            with:
              python-version: "3.13"

          - name: Install toymath and pytest
            run: |
              python -m pip install --upgrade pip
              pip install . pytest

          - name: Run the tests
            run: pytest
    ```

    Each step starts with a `-` and has an optional `name`, which is what
    you'll see on GitHub. The steps run in order. There are two kinds of
    steps:

    * Steps with `run` execute commands on the command line of the runner,
      just like you would in your terminal. The `|` lets us put several
      commands on separate lines.
    * Steps with `uses` run an *action*: a reusable piece of code that someone
      else wrote to do a common task. The text after `uses` is the GitHub
      repository the action lives in followed by `@` and the version to use;
      e.g., `actions/checkout@v7` is version 7 of
      https://github.com/actions/checkout. Some actions take inputs, which are
      given in the `with` section.

    Remember that each job runs on a brand new computer with nothing on it. So
    our job has to do everything you did on your computer to run the tests:

    * `actions/checkout` downloads a copy of your repository onto the runner.
    * `actions/setup-python` installs Python (version 3.13, in this case).
    * We then use `pip` to install `toymath` and `pytest`. (We don't need the
      `-e` here, since we won't be editing the code on the runner.)
    * Finally, we run `pytest`. If any of the tests fail, `pytest` will exit
      with an error, which will cause the job to fail.

    ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon="false"}
    ##### Check your work: the complete `tests.yml`

    ```yaml
    name: Tests

    on:
      push:
        branches: [main]
      pull_request:

    jobs:
      test:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - name: Check out the repository
            uses: actions/checkout@v7

          - name: Set up Python
            uses: actions/setup-python@v7
            with:
              python-version: "3.13"

          - name: Install toymath and pytest
            run: |
              python -m pip install --upgrade pip
              pip install . pytest

          - name: Run the tests
            run: pytest
    ```
    :::

### 6. Commit and push, then open a pull request

1.  Commit the workflow:

    ```bash
    git add .github/workflows/tests.yml
    git commit -m "add workflow to run tests"
    ```

2.  Push your branch to your fork on GitHub. Since `add-ci-tests` doesn't exist
    on GitHub yet, we need to tell `git` to create it:

    ```bash
    git push -u origin add-ci-tests
    ```

3.  Go to your fork on GitHub (`https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/toymath`).
    You should see a box saying that `add-ci-tests` had recent pushes. Click the
    green `Compare & pull request` button.

4.  This will open the "Comparing changes" page. **Look carefully at the gray
    box at the top of the page.** You'll see that the "base repository" is
    `SU-OSPO/toymath`. When you create a pull request from a fork, GitHub
    assumes by default that you want to contribute your changes back to the
    *upstream* repository you forked from. We don't want that here! We want to
    merge the changes into the `main` branch of *your* fork. To change that:

    * Click the "base repository: SU-OSPO/toymath" drop-down button and select
      `YOUR_USERNAME/toymath`.
    * The page will reload, and the gray box will now just show
      `base: main` ← `compare: add-ci-tests`. Make sure that `base` is `main`
      and `compare` is `add-ci-tests`.

    ::: {.callout-warning}
    Always double-check the base repository and branch before you create a pull
    request from a fork. It's easy to accidentally open a pull request on
    someone else's repository!
    :::

5.  Click the green `Create pull request` button.

::: {.callout-note}
If this is the first time you've used GitHub Actions on your fork, you might
see a message on the Actions tab saying that workflows aren't being run on
this forked repository. If so, click the green button saying "I understand my
workflows, go ahead and enable them." (GitHub disables workflows on forks by
default, since you didn't write them yourself.)
:::

### 7. Look at the results

1.  Scroll to the bottom of your pull request. Just above the merge button,
    you'll see a box that lists the *checks* on the pull request. You should
    see a check called `Tests / test (pull_request)`: this is the `Tests`
    workflow, `test` job, triggered by the `pull_request` event. While it's
    running it will have a yellow dot next to it. After a minute or so it
    should change to a green check mark, and the box will say "All checks have
    passed."

2.  Click on the `Tests / test (pull_request)` check. This will take you to
    the page for that run of the job. You'll see each of the steps you wrote in
    your workflow file (plus a few that GitHub adds automatically). Click on
    the "Run the tests" step to expand it. You'll see the same output from
    `pytest` that you saw on your computer!

3.  You can also see all of your workflow runs by clicking the `Actions` tab at
    the top of your repository's page on GitHub. Try that now. You'll see a
    list of all your workflows on the left, and all the times they've run in
    the middle.

## IV. Breaking things

Your tests pass. But how do you know that they actually test anything? Let's
see what happens when someone makes a change that breaks the code.

### 8. Introduce a bug

1.  Use your favorite text editor to open `toymath/functions.py`, and change
    the `+` in the `add` function to a `*`, so that it reads:

    ```python
    def add(a, b):
        """Return the sum of a and b."""
        return a * b
    ```

    Oops.

2.  Let's pretend that you forgot to run the tests on your computer before
    committing. Commit and push the change:

    ```bash
    git add -u
    git commit -m "update add function"
    git push
    ```

    (Since we used `-u` the first time we pushed, `git push` knows to push to
    the `add-ci-tests` branch on your fork.)

3.  Go back to your pull request on GitHub. Pushing to the `add-ci-tests`
    branch automatically updated the pull request, which triggered the `Tests`
    workflow again. Once it finishes, you should see a red X next to the check,
    and the box will say "All checks have failed."

4.  Click on the failed check, and expand the "Run the tests" step. You'll see
    that `pytest` tells you exactly what went wrong:

    ```bash
    >           assert subtract(c, a) == b
    E           assert 12 == 5
    E            +  where 12 = subtract(15, 3)
    ```

    Our round-trip test found that `add(3, 5)` returned `15` instead of `8`.

Notice that GitHub still lets you merge the pull request even though the
tests failed. Failing checks are a big red warning sign to anyone
reviewing the pull request, though!

::: {.callout-tip}
Many projects set up *branch protection rules* to prevent pull requests from
being merged until all the checks pass. You can do this in your repository's
Settings, under "Rules" (or "Branches"). See GitHub's documentation on
[protected branches](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches)
for more details.
:::

### 9. Fix the bug

1.  Open `toymath/functions.py` again and change the `*` back to a `+`.

2.  This time, run the tests on your computer before committing:

    ```bash
    pytest
    ```

    They should pass. (Try running `pytest` with the `*` in place, too, if you
    like. You'll see that you could've caught the bug before pushing it!)

3.  Commit and push the fix:

    ```bash
    git add -u
    git commit -m "fix add function"
    git push
    ```

4.  Go back to your pull request. Once the workflow finishes running, your
    checks should be green again.

## V. Testing on multiple operating systems and Python versions

Right now we only test on one operating system (Ubuntu Linux) and one version
of Python (3.13). But people who use your package will use lots of different
operating systems and versions of Python. Code that works on one doesn't
always work on another. (File paths are a common culprit: Windows uses `\`
to separate directories, whereas Linux and MacOS use `/`.)

Installing a bunch of different operating systems and versions of Python on
your own computer to test all of those combinations would be a pain. With
GitHub Actions it's easy, thanks to the *matrix* strategy.

### 10. Add a matrix to the workflow

1.  Open `.github/workflows/tests.yml` and change the `jobs` section so that it
    reads:

    ```yaml
    jobs:
      test:
        strategy:
          fail-fast: false
          matrix:
            os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
            python-version: ["3.12", "3.13", "3.14"]
        runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
        steps:
          - name: Check out the repository
            uses: actions/checkout@v7

          - name: Set up Python ${{ matrix.python-version }}
            uses: actions/setup-python@v7
            with:
              python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}

          - name: Install toymath and pytest
            run: |
              python -m pip install --upgrade pip
              pip install . pytest

          - name: Run the tests
            run: pytest
    ```

    Here's what changed:

    * We added a `strategy` section with a `matrix`. The matrix defines two
      variables, `os` and `python-version`, each with a list of values. GitHub
      will create a separate job for *every combination* of these values. In
      this case that's 3 operating systems × 3 Python versions = 9 jobs, all of
      which will run at the same time.
    * The `${{ ... }}` syntax lets us use the values of variables in the
      workflow. We use `${{ matrix.os }}` to set the operating system the job
      runs on, and `${{ matrix.python-version }}` to set which version of
      Python is installed.
    * By default, if one job in a matrix fails, GitHub cancels all the others.
      Setting `fail-fast: false` tells GitHub to let them all finish. That way
      we can see *all* of the combinations that fail, not just the first one.

    ::: {.callout-note}
    Why are the Python versions in quotes? Because YAML would otherwise read
    them as numbers, and `3.10` (for example) would become `3.1`!
    :::

2.  Commit and push the change:

    ```bash
    git add -u
    git commit -m "test on multiple operating systems and python versions"
    git push
    ```

3.  Go back to your pull request on GitHub. You'll now see nine checks at the
    bottom, with names like `Tests / test (macos-latest, 3.14) (pull_request)`.
    It might take a few minutes for all of them to finish (the Windows and
    MacOS runners are usually a bit slower to start). Click on a few of them to
    see the output. Go to the `Actions` tab too; if you click on the latest run
    of the `Tests` workflow you'll see all nine jobs listed on the left.

### 11. Merge the pull request

Assuming all of the checks pass, it's time to merge. Since we have a few
"oops" commits on this branch (breaking and then fixing the `add` function),
this is a good place to squash and merge (see the 9/17 lecture in the
[git unit](../02_git/index.qmd#lectures) if you need a refresher). Squashing
will combine all of the commits on `add-ci-tests` into a single commit on
`main`, so those "oops" commits won't clutter up `main`'s history.

1.  At the bottom of your pull request, click the drop-down arrow next to the
    green merge button and select "Squash and merge."

2.  Edit the commit message if you like, then click `Confirm squash and merge`.

3.  Click the `Delete branch` button to delete `add-ci-tests` on GitHub.

4.  Click on the `Actions` tab. You'll see that the `Tests` workflow is running
    again. This is because merging the pull request pushed a new commit to
    `main`, and we told the workflow to run on every push to `main`. That way
    you'll know if something on `main` ever gets broken, even if it gets there
    without a pull request.

## VI. Using a workflow template

Writing workflows from scratch is good for understanding how they work, but
you don't always need to. GitHub provides a library of *workflow templates*
for common tasks. Let's use one to add a workflow that runs
[Pylint](https://pylint.readthedocs.io) on our code. Pylint is a *linter*: a
program that checks your code for style problems and common mistakes (e.g.,
missing docstrings, unused variables, poorly named variables) without running
it.

This time, we'll do everything on GitHub, without touching our local
repository.

### 12. Create a branch on GitHub

1.  Go to your fork on GitHub (`https://github.com/YOUR_USERNAME/toymath`).
    Click the drop-down button that says `main` in the upper left, then click
    "View all branches."

2.  Click the green `New branch` button. In the "New branch name" field type
    `add-pylint`. Make sure the source is `main` (on *your* fork), then click
    `Create new branch`.

3.  **Switch to the new branch.** Go back to your fork's main page (click on
    `<> Code` at the top), click the branch drop-down button that says `main`,
    and select `add-pylint`. The drop-down button should now say `add-pylint`.
    This is important! We want to add the new workflow to the `add-pylint`
    branch, not to `main`.

### 13. Add the Pylint workflow

1.  Click on the `Actions` tab at the top of your repository, then click the
    `New workflow` button on the left. This will bring you to the "Choose a
    workflow" page, which lists templates that GitHub thinks may be relevant to
    your repository.

2.  In the search box, type `pylint`. Find the "Pylint" workflow and click its
    `Configure` button.

3.  This will open GitHub's file editor with a new file called
    `.github/workflows/pylint.yml`. Check the top of the page: next to the file
    name it should say you're editing on the `add-pylint` branch. You'll see
    something like this:

    ```yaml
    name: Pylint

    on: [push]

    jobs:
      build:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        strategy:
          matrix:
            python-version: ["3.8", "3.9", "3.10"]
        steps:
        - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        - name: Set up Python ${{ matrix.python-version }}
          uses: actions/setup-python@v3
          with:
            python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
        - name: Install dependencies
          run: |
            python -m pip install --upgrade pip
            pip install pylint
        - name: Analysing the code with pylint
          run: |
            pylint $(git ls-files '*.py')
    ```

    You should recognize most of this now! A few things to note:

    * This workflow runs on every push to *any* branch (`on: [push]`).
    * The last step uses `git ls-files '*.py'` to get a list of all the Python
      files in the repository, then runs `pylint` on them.
    * The template is a bit out of date: it uses older versions of the
      `checkout` and `setup-python` actions, and versions of Python that have
      reached their [end of life](https://devguide.python.org/versions/).
      Templates are a starting point; you'll often need to tweak them.

4.  Let's update the template. In the editor, change:

    * the `python-version` list to `["3.12", "3.13", "3.14"]`,
    * `actions/checkout@v4` to `actions/checkout@v7`, and
    * `actions/setup-python@v3` to `actions/setup-python@v7`.

5.  Click the green `Commit changes...` button in the upper right. Leave the
    default commit message, and make sure "Commit directly to the `add-pylint`
    branch" is selected. Then click `Commit changes`.

    ::: {.callout-warning}
    If the commit dialog says "Commit directly to the **`main`** branch"
    instead, you did not switch to the `add-pylint` branch before clicking
    on the `Actions` tab. Don't commit to `main`! Instead, select "Create a new
    branch for this commit and start a pull request," name the new branch
    `add-pylint-workflow`, and use that branch for the rest of this section.
    (You can delete the empty `add-pylint` branch afterward.)
    :::

6.  Click on the `Actions` tab. You'll see that `Pylint` is now listed as one of
    your workflows on the left, and that it's already running. That's because
    committing the file pushed a new commit to the `add-pylint` branch, and the
    workflow runs on every push.

### 14. Open a pull request and merge

1.  Go back to your fork's main page. You should see a box saying that
    `add-pylint` had recent pushes; click the `Compare & pull request` button.
    (If you don't see the box, click the `Pull requests` tab, then the green
    `New pull request` button, and select `add-pylint` as the `compare` branch.)

2.  **Again, change the base repository to `YOUR_USERNAME/toymath`**, so that
    you're merging `add-pylint` into the `main` branch of *your* fork, not
    the upstream repository. Then click `Create pull request`.

3.  Scroll to the bottom of the pull request. In addition to the nine `Tests`
    checks, you'll see three new `Pylint` checks, one for each version of
    Python. (Notice that these end with `(push)` rather than `(pull_request)`,
    since that's the event that triggered them.) Click on one of them and
    expand the "Analysing the code with pylint" step. If all goes well, you
    should see:

    ```bash
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    Your code has been rated at 10.00/10
    ```

    If Pylint finds *anything* to complain about, it will exit with an error,
    and the check will fail.

4.  Once you're happy with it, merge the pull request (a normal merge is fine
    here, since there's only one commit), then delete the `add-pylint` branch.

## VII. Wrapping up

Your fork's `main` branch on GitHub now has two new commits that your local
repository doesn't know about. Let's sync them.

1.  In your terminal, switch back to `main` and pull the changes:

    ```bash
    git checkout main
    git pull
    ```

    Run `ls .github/workflows`. You should see both `tests.yml` and
    `pylint.yml`.

2.  Delete your local copy of the `add-ci-tests` branch:

    ```bash
    git branch -D add-ci-tests
    ```

    Note that we had to use a capital `-D` here. That's because we squashed
    the commits on `add-ci-tests` when we merged, so `git` doesn't see the
    individual commits on that branch in `main`. It'll warn you that the
    branch isn't fully merged if you use `-d`. The capital `-D` forces the
    deletion.

Congratulations! Your repository now automatically runs its tests on three
operating systems and three versions of Python, and checks the code with a
linter, every time someone opens a pull request. In the [next
tutorial](tutorial2.qmd) we'll use GitHub Actions to build and publish
documentation for `toymath`.
